entries.title: Iraq bars Iranian football team’s plane from landing in Basra: Report
entries.summary: Decision by the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority reportedly related to ⁠US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines.
entries.content:
Decision by the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority reportedly related to ⁠US sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines.

Iraq barred a plane carrying Iran’s national football ⁠team from ⁠landing at Basra airport on Tuesday, a decision by the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority linked to ⁠sanctions by the United States imposed on Iranian airlines, two Basra airport officials told the Reuters news agency.

The plane returned to Iran and landed ⁠at Abadan airport, and the team will now travel by road to Basra, an Iranian consulate official in Basra said.

The Iranian team was travelling to Iraq to participate in a ‌four-nation tournament in Basra also involving Iraq, Lebanon and Palestine.

An Iraqi civil aviation official said Iraq made the decision because it could not risk violating US sanctions on Iranian airlines.

The incident highlights the increasing impact of US sanctions on Iranian aviation operations in Iraq. ⁠

Washington announced sanctions on any global companies doing business with Iranian airlines after September 23, aiming to ground Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide.

In September, Iraq ordered the suspension of Iranian flights to Baghdad airport after the US threatened secondary sanctions against airports and service providers that handle Iranian carriers.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that airports servicing Iranian airlines could face sanctions, including exclusion from the US ‌dollar system.

This warning was part of a broader effort to tighten restrictions on Iran’s transport sector and on ‌foreign ‌entities providing services to sanctioned Iranian airlines.

Intensified sanctions are part of a US bid to squeeze Iran economically as President Donald Trump struggles to end the war that the US and Israel launched on the country in February.

entries.title: FIA chief says Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix to go ahead despite tensions
entries.summary: This year's Saudi Arabian Grand Prix was scrapped following the outbreak of the US and Israel's war with Iran.
entries.content:
This year’s Saudi Arabian Grand Prix was scrapped following the outbreak of the US and Israel’s war with Iran.

The final races of the Formula One (F1) season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as planned despite tensions in the Middle East, the president of motorsports’ governing body Mohammed Ben Sulayem has said.

The last two grands prix of the year are scheduled for November 29 in Qatar and December 6 in Abu Dhabi.

The Saudi Arabia Grand Prix earlier this year was scrapped following the outbreak of the United States and Israel’s war with Iran, while the Bahrain race was delayed and moved to Malaysia.

“We are ready for Qatar and Abu Dhabi,” said Ben Sulayem, president of the Federation Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA), on social media on Tuesday.

“We are fully prepared and committed to delivering two outstanding grands prix weekends and a spectacular conclusion to the Formula One World Championship.

“We look forward to welcoming drivers, teams and fans to two iconic circuits for an unforgettable finish to the season. See you on the grid.”

Ben Sulayem’s comments echo those made by F1 boss Stefano Domenicali last month.

F1 drivers have expressed mixed feelings about racing in the Middle East, with four-time world champion Max Verstappen among those to air his reservations.

Italian youngster Kimi Antonelli has already wrapped up the drivers’ world championship title, while his Mercedes team secured the constructors’ crown last weekend in Sao Paulo.

Several events in Saudi Arabia, which borders Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, have been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by Yemen’s Houthis.

entries.title: Meta’s AI age-check goes global: Can it protect teens?
entries.summary: The tech giant rolls out age-detection tool for Instagram and Facebook, but experts doubt whether it can help protect teens.
entries.content:
The tech giant rolls out age-detection tool for Instagram and Facebook but experts doubt if it can help protect teenagers.

Meta has rolled out artificial intelligence (AI)-powered age-estimation technology worldwide in an effort to better detect teenage users who signed up for its social media platforms with an adult’s birth date.

The world’s largest social media company announced the change on Monday, saying that millions more young people worldwide would be placed in its Teen Accounts following the implementation of the new technology amid concerns that its platforms have failed to protect teenagers.

Teen Accounts have more restrictions and protections designed to provide a safer user experience. They keep the account private by default, limit content types, and prevent strangers from sending direct messages (DMs) to teenage account holders. Parents can also supervise Teen Accounts.

Experts, however, doubt whether the latest step will protect children from online harm.

Here’s what we know about the latest tool and why Meta has deployed it:

What has Meta announced?

Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, said on Monday that it had started using its AI age-estimation system on Instagram accounts around the world.

“Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally,” the company said.

The system is designed to identify teenagers who signed up with a fake birth date in order to use a regular account. They are then switched to a restricted Teen Account or removed from the platform.

Meta is also rolling out the new age-detection tool for Facebook and plans to implement a similar system worldwide for Threads, another of its social media apps, before the end of the year.

Before Monday, the system had already been rolled out in more than 20 countries. Meta has called on competitors to adopt similar age checks.

How will age checks work, and what protections will they trigger?

Meta says its AI judges whether an account holder is likely to be a teenager, regardless of what birth date they gave when signing up.

The AI searches a user’s account to find “contextual clues” that point to their age. Examples given by Meta include “birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades”.

It also uses “visual cues” in pictures and videos on the account, but Meta says that this does not extend to facial recognition.

Flagged accounts are then moved into Teen Accounts – on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger – which limit how long teenagers can spend on the apps, which content they can access, and who they can message.

In countries that ban social media for users under a certain age, the account may be shut down entirely.

In the United States, Meta will add specific restrictions for under-18s, capping their time on its apps at two hours a day and imposing a midnight-to-6am curfew.

In Australia, the firm says it has started using an Apple feature that verifies a user’s age range when their phone is set up and passes that on to apps they download.

Meta said it supports legislation that would have app stores verify users’ ages, calling it “more effective” than having many developers devising methods to collect the information for each app.

Why is Meta introducing these measures now?

In its announcement, Meta linked the new policy to the outcome of a groundbreaking lawsuit brought by 29 US states and cosigned by 52 US attorneys general.

The company was accused of designing Facebook and Instagram to addict children and collect their personal data, not doing enough to verify users’ ages and even encouraging minors to bypass its existing verification measures.

The suit was settled out of court in August, with Meta agreeing to pay up to $18bn to plaintiffs and to make significant changes to its platform to protect minors, including time limits, nighttime curfews and limits on filters that simulate cosmetic procedures.

Although Meta’s announcement cites the August out-of-court settlement, it has faced two other major legal actions in the US this year relating to the impact of its products on children.

In March, Meta was ordered to pay $375m when a New Mexico court found the company had been misleading about the safety of its platform for minors.

Around the same time, Meta and Google also lost a landmark case in Los Angeles, brought by a woman who said she had become addicted to Instagram and YouTube and faced mental health problems as a result.

Governments have also increasingly intervened to protect minors from what they see as the harms of social media.

In recent years, several countries have introduced social media bans for minors under a certain age, including the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Australia and Turkiye, with many more weighing similar measures.

Is this new system enough?

Sonia Livingstone, a professor at the London School of Economics and director of the Digital Futures for Children Centre, told Al Jazeera that Meta had yet to deliver evidence that its system was preventing underage users from using its platforms.

She pointed to an “absence of clear evidence” that young children could not create accounts or that teenagers who use the platforms were indeed being placed in Teen Accounts.

Livingstone said that Meta’s age check system “poses a privacy risk to all users, not just children, since the point of age assurance is to figure out who the children are”.

Without independent audits to determine how it works, “it is hard to see why we should trust them with our personal data”, she said.

Although Australia banned under-16s from social media in December, its regulator, eSafety, found that more than 80 percent of preteens and young teens were still using it half a year later, largely because age checks failed to stop them.

In that same period, Meta had shut down 462,000 Instagram accounts in compliance with the ban – but eSafety found that more than 69 percent of underage users retained their Instagram accounts.

There is also the risk that teenage users simply migrate to another platform that contains similar risks to their health.

Under the $18bn August settlement, about $5bn of Meta’s payment is conditional on its competitors, including TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat, agreeing to similar measures and payments.

Many of these platforms are also facing regulatory heat for similar issues to Meta. On Friday, European Union regulators threatened to fine TikTok owner ByteDance 6 percent of its global annual revenue for its addictive design.

EU tech commissioner Henna Virkunnen said the platform was “leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from” and called on TikTok to “step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors”.

entries.title: Who is Jean Leonard Teganya, deported by US over Rwanda genocide claims?
entries.summary: Teganya, a former medical student, is accused of participating in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda.
entries.content:
Teganya, a former medical student, is accused of participating in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda.

Jean Leonard Teganya, a former medical student accused of helping identify Tutsi civilians who were later killed during Rwanda’s 1994 genocide, has been deported from the United States to Rwanda, where he faces separate allegations of genocide and crimes against humanity.

Rwanda’s National Public Prosecution Authority (NPPA) confirmed that Teganya arrived at Kigali International Airport on the evening of November 9, 2026, accompanied by US security officers. He was handed over to Rwandan prosecutors.

The NPPA said it had indicted him in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocide and crimes against humanity in the former Butare prefecture in southern Rwanda. It did not provide details of the specific allegations against him.

Who is Teganya?

Born in 1971, Teganya was studying medicine at the National University of Rwanda in Butare during the genocide. He was also undertaking practical training at the University Teaching Hospital of Butare.

He left Rwanda in July 1994, as the genocide came to an end. According to US court records, he travelled through what was then Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as well as Kenya and India, before reaching Canada in 1999.

He applied for asylum in Canada, but his application was rejected in 2002 and again in 2012. The Canadian authorities’ decision, as described in the US appeal judgement, was based on the conclusion that he would not have survived in Rwanda in 1994 if he had not been perceived as sharing the intention to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.

After about 15 years of proceedings in Canada, Teganya evaded a deportation order and crossed into the United States on foot on August 3, 2014, near Houlton, Maine. He was taken into custody and applied for asylum.

What is he accused of?

The allegations against Teganya concern his conduct at the University Teaching Hospital of Butare during the genocide.

According to evidence presented by US prosecutors at his 2019 trial, Teganya was affiliated with the National Republican Movement for Democracy and Development (MRND), the ruling political party at the time, and the Interahamwe militia associated with it.

The US Department of Justice said trial evidence showed that Teganya led groups of soldiers and Interahamwe members through the hospital to search for Tutsi patients and refugees hiding there. Those discovered were taken away and killed behind the maternity ward, according to the prosecution’s account.

The prosecution also presented evidence linking him to the killing of three Tutsi people at the hospital and Tutsi students in university accommodation. It further alleged that he participated in five rapes involving two Tutsi women who had sought shelter at the hospital.

These allegations formed part of the evidence in his US immigration-related trial. They should not be confused with the specific charges in Rwanda’s separate case against him, which have not been detailed publicly.

Why was he convicted in the United States?

Teganya was not tried for genocide in the United States. The criminal case concerned statements he made to US immigration authorities.

Prosecutors accused him of concealing his political affiliations and activities during the genocide when seeking asylum.

In September 2017, he was indicted on two counts of immigration fraud and three counts of perjury. A federal jury convicted him on all five counts on April 5, 2019.

He was sentenced to 97 months in prison on July 1, 2019. The sentence included an enhancement for obstruction of justice based on his false testimony during the trial.

Teganya appealed, but the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit upheld his convictions and sentence in May 2021.

His US convictions were for immigration fraud and perjury, not genocide. The allegations about his conduct during the genocide featured in the evidence presented at trial, but the jury did not convict him of genocide.

Why does Rwanda want him?

Rwanda’s prosecution authority says it indicted Teganya in 2014 over alleged genocide and crimes against humanity committed in the former Butare prefecture.

His return allows Rwandan authorities to pursue that separate case in the country where the alleged crimes took place.

However, the NPPA’s public statement did not set out the individual allegations or specify when Teganya would appear in court. It would therefore be premature to assume that every allegation presented during his US trial forms part of the Rwandan indictment.

Why does his case matter?

Teganya’s return brings him back to Rwanda to face allegations that have remained unresolved in its judicial system since 2014.

His case has crossed three legal systems: Canada’s examination of his eligibility for asylum, the US prosecution over false statements in immigration proceedings, and Rwanda’s separate allegations of genocide and crimes against humanity.

More than three decades after the genocide, the question now is whether Rwandan prosecutors can establish his individual responsibility for the crimes of which he is accused. His return does not amount to a conviction, and he will have the opportunity to defend himself in court.

entries.title: Israeli soldiers are also settlers in West Bank: Al Jazeera investigation
entries.summary: Blurred lines between Israeli soldiers and settlers fuel systematic West Bank violence and mass displacement.
entries.content:
An Al Jazeera investigation reveals how blurred lines between Israeli soldiers and West Bank settlers enable systematic violence, land seizures, and mass displacement.

Israeli settlers carrying out pogroms in the occupied West Bank often also then return dressed in military uniforms to impose orders on Palestinian victims, blurring the lines between violent attackers and security forces Israel claims uphold the law, an Al Jazeera investigation has found.

The incidents captured in the investigation bolster the evidence presented by many Palestinian communities, international and Israeli human rights groups, activists and journalists pointing to institutional Israeli backing for settlers who have attacked, burned and taken over entire villages.

A particularly stark example played out in the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus.

Through facial matching and local testimonies, the investigation identified Yitzhak Levi Filant, a settler from Yitzhar known locally as “Yaqoub”. Filant was documented assaulting farmers in civilian clothing, only to return to the same village wearing a military uniform, carrying a military-issued weapon and issuing orders to residents.

Filant was placed on the United States sanctions list in August 2024 under President Joe Biden before President Donald Trump’s administration removed him from the list in early 2025.

Abbas Melhem, director of the Palestinian Farmers Union, told Al Jazeera that this duality is a daily reality. “When the farmer says, for example, to a settler: ‘I will call the army,’ the settler tells him: ‘There is no need for that.’ He goes to his car, then puts on his military uniform and returns and tells him: ‘I am the army!'” Melhem said.

“The army in the West Bank and the settlers are two sides of the same coin, and they serve the same goal planned and implemented by the Israeli government through this system,” Melhem added.

Lethal dual identities

The investigation documented deadlier manifestations of this overlap in Hebron. On March 7, a settler named Nahman encroached on Palestinian land near the Susya settlement and summoned reinforcements. An off-road vehicle soon arrived with the brothers Shem Tov and Luria Luski. Luria Luski, who has appeared in military uniform in other footage, opened fire. The attack killed Amir Shanaran, a resident, and severely wounded his cousin.

Shanaran’s father recounted the harrowing scene to Al Jazeera. “The first two shots in the air, bang, and then he came to my nephew, hit him with the muzzle of the rifle in his face here. I came and tried to defend my nephew. Shem Tov came and hit me in my head with the stick. I fell,” the father stated. “My late son, may God have mercy on him, Amir, came. He came to defend me. He pushed the settler away from me. He shot him on the spot,” he added.

Israeli attacks in the West Bank have escalated rapidly since October 7, 2023, and the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel. They were followed by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

According to the Al Jazeera investigation, 14 of 63 Palestinians killed by settlers since October 7, 2023, were shot by individuals serving in the army or wearing military uniforms.

Additional footage showed soldier Bezalel Talia raiding Palestinian homes and detaining residents while simultaneously running a training camp for settler youth involved in attacks on villages.

Institutional cover

This coordination is structurally supported by the Israeli military’s Regional Defence battalions, known as Hagmar. These units have expanded sixfold since 2023, shifting their core function from guarding settlements to backing settler operations. Assaf Surya, the battalions’ deputy commander in Hebron, acknowledged in an interview with Israeli media that most Hagmar members are settlers serving in the reserves.

Mohannad Mustafa, an expert on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that the force’s mission has fundamentally changed. “Because it enjoys political support and it was originally armed in order to be a tool in the colonial settlement project in the West Bank, … therefore, it was armed by the army, and it was armed by the Israeli Ministry of National Security, and it was supported politically, and it was supported economically also and financially by the Israeli government,” Mustafa said.

“Part of the idea of defending the settlements now has become geographical expansion, expelling the Palestinians from their lands and restricting them,” Mustafa explained.

Gideon Levy, a writer and journalist at the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, analysed the deliberate nature of this integration. “The settlers made the decision to enter into the Israeli army and specifically in the units stationed in the West Bank,” Levy noted to Al Jazeera. “We have seen gradually and systematically an increasing number of commanders who are settlers themselves.”

Systemic impunity

The investigation revealed that weapons flow through both official military service and government facilitation: National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has said that at least 120,000 civilian weapon licences have been issued to settlers during the current government’s tenure. Training occurs at settlement firing ranges, such as the Ma’on settlement facility.

Amir Daoud from the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission highlighted the severe security implications: “This is also what happened over the past years, that many security officers who were working for many years in security apparatuses and resigned or retired from them, joined settler militias and made a lot of information available to settler militias in order to use it against the Palestinians.”

This militarised network has enabled settlers to seize control of about one-fifth of the West Bank and force the displacement of 118 Palestinian communities under the current government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

During these operations, official forces frequently do not intervene.

“A farmer was killed by a settler weeks ago, and again, the army was there, and the army remained standing idly by and did not help the farmer and did not hold the killers accountable, and they were not brought to justice,” Levy said of an incident in Yasuf.

Melhem agreed.

“Most of the olives that were stolen this year – and we are talking so far about around 50 tonnes – were with the participation of the army, and … much of these olives were transported in the military cars themselves,” he noted.

Itamar Avneri, a founding member of the Israeli grassroots movement Standing Together, told Al Jazeera the Netanyahu government “encourages the settlers and encourages the Israeli army and gives them a blank cheque in order to commit these crimes and escape any punishment”.

According to Avneri, “a large number of soldiers in the army participate in the attacks because they believe that there is no partner on the other side.” These soldiers, he added, “know that they will escape punishment”.

Accountability remains virtually nonexistent. The Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported that 93.6 percent of settler criminal cases opened by police since 2005 have been closed without indictments.

“I was surprised that they investigated 7 percent of the cases,” Levy said. “If the Israeli soldier shoots a dog tomorrow and if the settler shoots the Palestinian, I believe that the soldier who shot the dog will be brought to justice quicker than that settler who shot targeting the farmer.”

For the family of Amir Shanaran, though, that distinction between a soldier and settler has already lost all meaning. They both carry the same weapons, receive the same protection and mean the same thing to Palestinian communities: violence, displacement, destruction and far too often death.

entries.title: Spain mulls TikTok suspension after investigation into child sex abuse videos
entries.summary: Ministry of Youth and Children calls for urgent meeting with TikTok leadership in Spain.
entries.content:
Ministry of Youth and Children calls for urgent meeting with TikTok leadership in Spain.

Spain is considering suspending TikTok after an independent investigation found more than 1,000 child sexual abuse videos on the platform with a total of 48 million views.

Spanish foundation Maldita.es said it detected more than 20,000 profiles of suspected paedophiles – 7,000 of them in Spanish – during the 35 days it monitored the popular video-blogging platform in September and October.

The nonprofit organisation, which aims to combat disinformation and promote transparency, also accused TikTok of amplifying content by minors in the algorithm, and profiting from their abuse.

“Abuse is not hidden away in a little corner and it is not hard to find,” Clara Jimenez Cruz, Maldita.es cofounder and chief executive, said.

During its investigation, “TikTok: Home to predators”, Maldita.es said it analysed profiles, comments and live broadcasts and created its own accounts to see how the algorithm responded.

It said that in just three days the algorithm recommended 19 livestreams by minors, including 15 in a single morning, all recorded from schools.

In one instance, Maldita.es said TikTok recommended a livestream from a 10-year-old girl in Spain who received suggestive comments from an adult male during the broadcast.

“Not only are [children] objectified, but they’re also asked to perform sexualised actions in exchange for TikTok gifts in the form of objects or animated animals that cost the user money,” Maldita.es said, claiming that the platform then takes a portion of the money spent, although the exact amount is unclear.

Spain’s Ministry of Youth and Children has demanded explanations from TikTok and raised the possibility of suspending the platform, which is owned by Chinese parent company ByteDance.

In a post on X, the ministry said it had asked prosecutors to take action over alleged cases of child sexual abuse on TikTok and that Minister Sira Rego had demanded an urgent meeting with the platform’s representatives in Spain.

‘Material you would expect to find only on the dark web’

The Maldita.es investigation identified 231 profiles that posted 1,183 explicit items of content, 780 accounts that use the network to attract buyers and more than 10,000 that ask for exchanges of sexual images in the comments.

When all the categories set out in the report were collated, the foundation said it detected some 26,000 accounts of suspected paedophiles, and had handed those details to authorities.

“Material you would expect to find only on the dark web is on TikTok,” Maldita.es said. “The findings of this investigation seriously call into question the effectiveness of TikTok’s measures against child abuse, and also point directly to its platform features being actively exploited by child predators.”

The organisation said that when its findings were published on Monday, TikTok had removed just one-tenth of the content it had flagged and had blocked only a quarter of illegal posts in Spain.

TikTok is facing a wave of lawsuits and investigations over accusations that it has failed to protect minors, accusations it has denied.

On Friday, the European Union told TikTok to change the “harmful” design of its personalised “For You” feed or risk large fines under the bloc’s digital content rules.

entries.title: Pentagon Chief Hegseth calls US House impeachment effort a ‘farce’
entries.summary: Hegseth condemns impeachment resolution against him as 'sabotage', defending his actions and policy decisions.
entries.content:
Hegseth condemns impeachment resolution against him as ‘sabotage’, defending his actions and policy decisions.

During a news conference, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has condemned impeachment efforts against him as “sabotage”.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt,” he said on Tuesday, calling criticism of him and the war on Iran “policy disagreements”.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth on Monday over the war on Iran, strikes on purported drug boats and other alleged violations of US laws.

“This is not patriotism, this is sabotage,” Hegseth said on Tuesday.

In a post on Truth Social after Hegseth spoke, US President Donald Trump defended Hegseth and his statements, saying he “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

The House of Representatives is likely to take an initial vote on the impeachment effort Tuesday, a procedural vote on whether to debate the impeachment resolution.

‘A job well done’

Speaking at his first news conference at the Pentagon in nearly six months, Hegseth defended his role in military actions ordered by President Trump.

Hegseth compared military losses under his tenure with other historic conflicts, saying some 60,000 Americans were killed in the Vietnam War, and 37,000 in the Korean War, while only 18 had been lost during the US-Israel war against Iran.

He addressed several of the issues raised in the impeachment resolution against him, including the lawfulness of strikes on alleged drug boats and the abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

The strikes on purported drug boats, Hegseth said, had been necessary to protect the US against narcotraffickers, and each strike had saved “thousands of American lives”. Maduro, the former president of Venezuela, Hegseth said, “was not kidnapped; he was brought to justice”.

“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” Hegseth said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when asked on Tuesday about the impeachment effort, also defended Hegseth, saying actions including the strikes on drug boats and the Iran war were in response to “imminent threats” to the US.

“The president of the United States is the commander in chief, and he has a right to defend this country and to address imminent threats that pose a threat to the United States, and he’s done so,” Rubio said.

Hegseth, Rubio added, had acted on “a direct order from the commander in chief, who in our constitution is empowered and trusted with the job of keeping Americans safe”.
